item.title: Whatever Happened to Implicit Attitudes?
item.description:
Bias

Whatever Happened to Implicit Attitudes?

Implicit bias was all the rage, and then it disappeared from public view. Why?

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • The early research in implicit bias got a lot of attention.
  • Measures of implicit attitudes had a lot of variability and did not predict much behavior.
  • Research explored whether the measures could be improved.
  • Current work suggests these measures may predict what is happening societally rather than individually.
Source: Image generated with Midjourney, 9/21/26

In the mid-1990s, there was an uptick in interest in the concept of implicit attitude (sometimes called implicit bias). A key motivation for this idea was the recognition that in industrialized nations like the United States, there had been a growing set of legal protections for historically marginalized groups like ethnic minorities that had led to decreases in overt acts of racism, but the overall social and economic position of members of those groups has not improved substantially.

One explanation for that observation is the prospect that people in these cultures have persistent prejudices that are not reflected in measurements of people’s overt attitudes. When asked about racist beliefs, for example, people may respond with sentiments of equality, but their actions may still be biased against group members in ways that maintain the status difference between groups.

These underlying attitudes, which are not reflected in explicit measures of prejudice, were called unconscious or sometimes implicit biases. The aim was primarily to distinguish them from biases that emerge from the application of a consciously held and applied belief. A 2026 paper by Keith Payne in the Annual Review of Psychology explored the current state of research on this topic.

Early research in this area focused on the development of tools to measure these implicit beliefs or attitudes. Many of the measures that were developed involved having people respond quickly to prompts and using their speed of reaction as a measure of the strength of relationship or association among concepts. The most widely studied of the many methods that were created was the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which had people do classification tasks interleaved. You can read more about this test and some of the concerns about its effectiveness here. For now, though, I’ll point out that an upshot of the research on techniques like this is that people’s performance on tasks like this is highly variable and ultimately does not predict much about their later behavior.

The observation that people may not score that similarly on tests of implicit associations from one administration to another (and that these tests do not predict people’s long-term behavior) led to a flurry of research exploring whether these measures reflect momentary changes in people’s engagement of biases. For example, it may be that aspects of a specific situation may drive people’s evaluation—in much the same way that a particular food may taste better when you need to eat than when you don’t. While this work is ongoing, it is unlikely that attitudes that change rapidly with context are likely to be the source of persistent prejudices.

A particularly interesting observation with these measures has led to a radically different interpretation. A number of studies reviewed in this paper have found that looking at trends across people in a region leads to greater prediction of group behaviors than looking at behavior of individuals. A study of bias measures at a country level found that countries that had a stronger relationship of males than females to science also had bigger gaps between school-age boys and girls in science performance. Similarly, within regions of a country, stronger levels of bias in implicit measures were correlated with acts of racial prejudice in those regions, including differences in overall health outcomes and overall levels of racial bias in likelihood of being stopped by the police.

The idea here is that particular ideas may be widely held within a region in ways that lead people in that region to quickly access those ideas. Those ideas may not influence the behavior of any particular individual, but on average they have their impact. That makes it difficult to use measures of implicit bias as predictors of the behavior of an individual, because it is more a marker of the prevalence of an idea in a society rather than a factor driving the specific actions someone takes.

This interpretation of these measures also suggests why many approaches to debiasing have been ineffective. After the rise of research on implicit biases, many companies spent significant amounts of money on training designed to identify and counteract implicit bias. These training programs did not have much influence on measures of bias or on behaviors. If measures of implicit bias are measuring something about the persistence of beliefs in a region, then education aimed at a small number of individuals may not have much impact.

When the idea of implicit attitudes was first raised in research, it captured a lot of the public imagination as well. The idea that societal prejudices were rooted in prejudices people were either not aware of or had no control over was powerful. As the research has matured, however, it is clear that this work captures something powerful but more mundane. There are powerful biases that operate in regions of the world. Everyone living in those areas is aware of those biases, and they influence how easily concepts related to bias can be accessed. But these powerful biases will also be complex to counteract, because they are a reflection of social forces rather than just an aggregation of individual behaviors.

item.title: Marcus Aurelius on Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

Marcus Aurelius on Anxiety

Learn the Stoic method for reducing anxiety.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety points towards the future: what might happen or go wrong.
  • We often try to outrun anxiety by keeping busy instead of confronting it.
  • Focus on what is within your control—and let go of what is not.
Antoine Bourdelle’s Herakles the Archer (1909) captures the Stoic ideal: complete commitment to the action, complete detachment from the outcome.
Source: Gaimard / Pixabay

Whereas depression weighs upon life as it is, anxiety points towards the future: what might happen, what might go wrong, what might be expected of us.

Of course, some concern for the future is necessary. It motivates us to do what’s needed, pay our bills, and avoid danger. So the aim cannot be to abolish anxiety altogether—simply to prevent occasional alarm from becoming a permanent state.

Modern Life

The modern world makes this difficult because threats are seldom all-or-nothing. Our ancestors faced a predator, or did not. We have emails, deadlines, mortgages. And when we look on social media, we feel we are falling behind.

Because the pressure is diffuse and continuous, we internalize it. Eventually, nobody needs to chase us; we carry the pursuer in our head.

Once the pursuer is inside us, we try to outrun them by keeping busy. Activity gives us a sense of control, but often we are not addressing the anxiety so much as preventing ourselves from feeling it. We run faster and faster so that we never have to ask where we are going.

A Zen story tells of a horseman galloping down a path at speed. It seemed as if the rider was on some urgent and vital mission.

“Where are you heading?” hollered a bystander.

“I don’t know!” came the already distant reply. “Ask the horse!”

How to Reduce Anxiety

The first step, then, is to stop running and name the anxiety. A vague anxiety can fill the whole sky; a named fear becomes one object within it. Once identified, it can be worked with, accepted, or dismissed.

In particular, we can determine what part of the anxiety is actually within our control. The ancient Stoics emphasized this distinction between what is and is not in our control. What is not in our control must simply be let go.

The Stoics had this image of an archer. The archer does all he can to shoot accurately. But once the arrow leaves the bow, its fate is no longer within the archer’s control. So the right-thinking archer focuses on the action, not on its result—because the first is in his control, whereas the other is not.

When dealing with our anxiety, we should all become like the Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius, who wrote, “Today I escaped anxiety. Or no, I discarded it, because it was within me, in my own perceptions—not outside.”

You may also be interested in my companion piece, The Root of All Anxiety.

item.title: Ongoing Personal Growth Means You're Going to Make Mistakes
item.description:
Perfectionism

Ongoing Personal Growth Means You're Going to Make Mistakes

Have self-compassion after making a wrong choice. Repair, learn, and grow.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Letting go of your expectations of perfection won't mean that you will stop having successes.
  • Perfectionism may have helped you gain achievements; you have likely also lost things along the way.
  • Notice if your perfectionistic expectations have impacted your expectations of others.

Are others allowed to make mistakes? Oftentimes the answer will be, “It depends.” We tend to consider the person’s intent, what they “should” have known, whether they apologized, how sincere the apology seemed, and its impact on others.

Our chronically online world, where everyone seems to be sharing a lot of personal information about themselves all of the time, has highlighted the reality that people constantly make mistakes. Some of this is unintentional, and sometimes it is very much intentional (i.e., rage-baiting so you will get angry and engage with their content). Nevertheless, this has an impact on a question of critical importance...

Source: Santa Barbara / Unsplash

Are you allowed to make mistakes?

I have coached many professional women who have contributed to their fields in impressive ways. I’ve noticed a pattern that they tend to be hypercritical of themselves when they make a mistake, in either their personal or professional lives. Sometimes these women make up only a small portion of their specialty and feel an additional pressure to demonstrate that women deserve to be there (especially in a leadership role).

I hear them speak about how they need to give 110 percent, always make others happy, and never mess up. The catch is that they usually have been successful in getting to where they are in their profession by aiming for and expecting perfection from themselves.

It’s incredibly hard to let go of perfectionism

Perfectionism is self-reinforcing, which makes it a hard habit to break. Why would you let go of a strategy that has gotten you through years of school and helped you start and build a successful career?

In response to that question, I would encourage you to respond and reflect on the following questions:

  • What has perfectionism given you?
  • What has perfectionism cost you?
  • How has perfectionism negatively impacted the way you view yourself, others, and the world?

If you have decided that your worth is tied to how well you can perform, it has likely fed into negative self-talk. You might catch yourself thinking things like “I’m so stupid” or “I should’ve known better.” It has also likely impacted the expectations you have of those around you (e.g., coworkers, your children).

  • Who benefits from you being stuck in this cycle of guilt, shame, and perfectionism?
  • Who taught you that you had to be perfect?
  • How would someone who has unconditional love for themself respond if they were told they should feel shame or guilt after making a mistake?

You likely learned from a young age that others around you would be happy with you or that you would be safer if you performed a certain way. What did the younger version of yourself learn about how they were allowed to show up in the world?

  • How would you support a loved one who has made a mistake? How is that different from how you would respond to yourself in the same situation?
  • What would you lose if you were kinder to yourself?
  • What would you gain if you were kinder to yourself?
  • How else could you motivate yourself?

If it feels too hard to be kind to yourself for your sake alone, consider what you intentionally want to model for those around you. As you reflect on your answers to these questions, be compassionate and gentle with yourself.

I’ll leave you with a quote from Stephen Sondheim’s musical Sunday in the Park with George: “The choice may have been mistaken, the choosing was not. Keep moving on.” Keep making choices. Keep making work that betters the world around you. Even if it’s not perfect or you learn a hard lesson, the choice may have been mistaken; the choosing was not. Keep moving on.

item.title: Interview Like a Boss
item.description:
Leadership

Interview Like a Boss

Practical strategies for landing a leadership role.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • A strong opening and closing can shape how interviewers remember a candidate.
  • Careful research leads to more relevant answers and more thoughtful questions in an interview.
  • Concise stories are a compelling way to demonstrate a your skills, abilities, and results in an interview.
  • The worst thing a leadership candidate can do is to rely on their resume, failing to prepare properly.

Congratulations! You were invited to an on-site interview for a leadership position! That, alone, is something to be proud of!

But interviewing for a leadership role is different from interviewing for an entry-level position. You may even have experience serving as the interviewer, but that does not automatically translate into being a great interviewee.

Interviewing involves skills that can be learned, practiced, and honed. The worst thing you can do is arrive unprepared and expect your résumé to speak for itself. This is the big leagues, kid. You need to do better than that.

Here are some actionable steps to take in the weeks leading up to your interview.

For an interview, dress one step above the organization's everyday norm.
Source: Feygrace / Pixabay

Do: Get there early, and dress the part!

This may seem obvious, but it’s worth stating: get there early. On time is late. 15 minutes early is on time. Give yourself enough time to find your bearings, use the restroom, and sit for a moment before being called back. You want to enter with a calm, steady mindset instead of the chaotic mindset that comes from rushing through the door at the last minute.

Dress the part, too. What is appropriate will depend on the workplace, but a good rule of thumb is to dress one step above the organization’s everyday norm. If employees typically wear slacks and button-down shirts, add a blazer. If the environment is generally casual, choose dress pants or slacks.

Keep your clothing, hair, makeup, jewelry, and accessories professional and relatively understated. Avoid anything so attention-grabbing that it competes with what you are saying. This is not the time to make a statement with your clothes or makeup. Your message should be the focus.

Don’t: Fumble the opening (or the closing!)

You can be pretty sure that every interview is going to begin with some version of these questions:

“Why are you interested in this job?”

“Why this specific company?”

“Why is right now the time for you?”

Make sure you have rock-solid answers to these questions lined up ahead of time, ready to go. For example, “This position aligns with my career interests, drawing on skills I have already demonstrated, and gives me an opportunity to make an even greater impact.”

It’s okay to be a real person and reference life circumstances where relevant. You might explain, “When my children were younger, I needed more flexibility with my schedule. Now that they’re older and more independent, I’m excited about the opportunity to dedicate myself more fully to this type of leadership role.” Be genuine and authentic, but do so in a way that is appropriate for the situation and doesn’t teeter into the realm of over-sharing.

Similarly, nearly every interview ends with some version of, “What questions do you have for us?”

Be prepared. Bring a printed list of thoughtful questions. They should demonstrate that you have researched the organization and seriously considered the role. Do not ask for information that is readily available on its website.

You can also turn an earlier interview question around. For example, if you were asked what you would do during your first 30 days, you might say, “I shared what I would prioritize during my first month. From your perspective, what are the most pressing issues the person in this role will need to address first?”

You can all but guarantee that both of these questions are going to be asked, so you better be prepared to start and end strong.

Do: Your research.

Research the role and the organization, but dig deeper than that. Do you know who will be interviewing you? Learn about the person and their role. Review their LinkedIn profile and search for projects, initiatives, or accomplishments connected to their work.

When relevant, incorporate that knowledge naturally into conversation. “One initiative that impressed me was the needs survey Judy conducted in 2025. I would be interested in building on those findings and using them to guide the next round of decisions.”

You may be surprised by how much useful information you can find on organizational websites and other public-facing platforms. That knowledge will help you ask better questions, tailor your examples, and demonstrate genuine interest in the position.

Don’t: Expect that your résumé speaks for itself.

Think of yourself as a politician. Ever notice how skilled politicians find ways to communicate their central message, regardless of the exact questions they are asked? You should do the same.

Think ahead of time of the main points you want to get across in the interview. These might include major accomplishments, leadership strengths, or skills that distinguish you from other candidates. Then practice weaving these points into your answers in ways that feel relevant and natural.

Do not assume your reputation precedes you or try to answer every question off the cuff. You may already hold a leadership role and believe this position is the next logical step. You may even think you are a shoo-in. But as the familiar saying goes, failing to prepare is preparing to fail.

Do: Prepare your stories.

Short story-based examples are always more compelling than long narrative diatribes. Because leadership interviews often include behavioral and scenario-based questions, think through several examples you are likely to encounter.

Some common examples include:

“Tell me about a time you had to work with a difficult client.”

“Tell me about a time you had to manage competing priorities.”

“How have you worked with stakeholders who had conflicting interests?”

Use the STAR method: situation, task, action, result. Briefly provide the context, explain your responsibility, describe what you did, and finish with the outcome. Keep your stories focused and concise, and you’ll end up looking like a star as a result!

A leadership interview is not simply a conversation about your past. It is an opportunity to help the interviewers picture you in the role. Your preparation should make that picture easy to see.

Know the message you want them to remember. Bring stories that demonstrate it. Ask questions that show you are already thinking like a leader. Then walk into the room calm, prepared, and ready to make your case.

Your résumé may have earned you the interview, but what you do in the room will earn you the job.

item.title: Why Pain Persists After Injury and How to Heal
item.description:
Chronic Pain

Why Pain Persists After Injury and How to Heal

Brain re-training techniques can lower pain.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • The brain can learn pain and produce it in the absence of injury or danger.
  • The brain can be re-trained to produce less pain.
  • Mental training strategies grounded in pain neuroscience can play a key role in a holistic pain recovery plan.
  • Pain is never all in your head — but you can re-train a hypersensitive nervous system.

A significant number of people experience pain that persists after an injury or surgery. When your medical team has told you that your injuries have healed, experiencing chronic pain can feel scary, frustrating, and confusing. It can be hard to find clear answers to the question: "Why do I still hurt, and what can I do about it?"

As I detail in my new book, Train Your Brain to Beat Chronic Pain, pain scientists’ understanding of chronic pain has evolved rapidly in recent decades, and new knowledge about the neuroscience of pain and pain recovery is only slowly reaching the public. This article unpacks key findings for people living with pain to consider as they navigate their own unique pain recovery journey. Of course, before embarking on any new treatments, consult your care team for personalized guidance.

Neuroplasticity and Pain

Believe it or not, the nervous system can “learn” pain. Just like you ride a bike without thinking about it after having done it for years, your nervous system can get really good at making pain. When you were injured, your brain produced a pain experience to motivate you to deal with your injury. Although it was unpleasant, pain was helpful to you. However, somewhere along the way, your pain “alarm” alerting you to threats became faulty. It became too sensitive.

How does this happen? Surprising though it may sound, all pain — even acute pain — is ultimately produced by the brain. That doesn’t mean that pain is “all in your head” — all pain is always real. But when you look at the brain’s role, you can unlock new avenues to treat your pain problem; you can re-train the brain.

Your brain doesn’t see the world as it really is. It can only make guesses about how safe or in danger you might be based on sensory and perceptual information. One piece of information is physical — for instance, the signals sent to the brain from the nerves in your arms and legs. Your thoughts, beliefs, feelings, social situation, environment, and behaviors are other types of information that the brain considers as it “decides” whether a pain experience is needed to aid your survival. For example, self-defeating thoughts, social isolation, and physical inactivity are all things that the brain would consider threatening — thus increasing the likelihood of pain. Pain isn’t just biological — it’s psychological and social as well.

Why does this happen? If we personify the brain, it’s as if your brain continues to “think” that your body might be in danger — in the absence of any real physical threats — and it’s warning you even though it doesn’t need to. This happened because of neuroplasticity. The brain can get really good — too good — at making pain.

Pain Therapies That Can Help Re-Train the Brain

The brain can unlearn pain. Here are three science-backed approaches that can help re-train the brain as part of a holistic, personalized pain recovery plan.

Pain Reprocessing Therapy

Pain Reprocessing Therapy is a science-backed treatment grounded in pain neuroscience. Key elements include learning about pain neuroscience and challenging inaccurate beliefs about pain. For example, hypothetical patient Joe might have chronic low back pain. MRI imaging has shown he has a slipped disc. That imaging finding may or may not be causing the pain. In fact, spinal degeneration tends to occur with increasing age, and lots of people with significant imaging findings feel no pain at all. Remember — correlation does not mean causation. Although a slipped disc and pain are happening at the same time, it doesn't mean the imaging finding is surely the cause of the pain. John's pain could be at least partially caused by an oversensitive pain alarm, and by retraining the brain, he could lower the pain.

Pain Reprocessing Therapy also involves practicing something called safety reappraisal, which is a mindfulness-based practice where participants learn to view their pain sensations as safe rather than dangerous. Pain sensations don’t necessarily reflect tissue damage; they reflect an oversensitive pain alarm.

Mindfulness

Practicing mindfulness meditation can help lower pain. A key mechanism of mindfulness for pain appears to be a reduction in the emotional enhancement of pain. For example, when your pain increases, you might think, “Here we go again. I hate this, and I probably will have to call off work tomorrow. I might end up losing my job soon.” You’re angry and sad. Negative emotions and catastrophic thoughts tend to worsen pain. Mindfulness practice encourages you to relate to your pain, thoughts, and emotions with an open, compassionate, and non-judgmental stance. You train yourself to look at pain through a lens of relative safety, rather than threat and reactivity.

Positive Psychology

Positive psychology is the science and practice of augmenting human strengths and virtues, including positive emotions and meaningful life pursuits. When you’re experiencing chronic pain, your brain becomes fixated on the pain and on threats. It fails to notice all the sources of safety and joy that are still all around you. Research shows that nurturing positive emotions and doing activities that could bring you joy can lower pain. Positive emotions are associated with a release of your body's internal painkillers — your body's natural pharmacy!

How can you increase pleasure and reward when you hurt all the time? Start with a brief savoring practice. The next time you do something that could bring you pleasure — like petting your dog, sitting outside in nature, or enjoying a meal with a friend — slow down and intentionally take in the sights, smells, sounds, textures, and physical sensations, and be open to receiving any positive feelings that may arise. Notice any signals of safety or joy that may be present. Open yourself to receiving these positive feelings; let them sink into you and fill you.

When chronic pain takes hold, your life can start to become incredibly small. You say no to social engagements and opportunities to be physically active. You wait for the pain to go away so that you can resume your life. However, filling your life with non-drug sources of reward, pleasure, and meaning is a key aspect of pain recovery. Pace yourself in collaboration with your care team.

Summary

It is possible to recover from chronic pain through a holistic, biopsychosocial approach that is grounded in modern pain neuroscience. Your pain is unique as you are — stay persistent on the path to recovery and collaborate with your care team. Find a mental health provider with chronic pain expertise to partner with you in your journey.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Gun Violence Hurts Everyone, Especially Children
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Gun Violence Hurts Everyone, Especially Children

It isn't just the victims or their families who are harmed by gun violence.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Gun violence has an impact on those who see it or hear it.
  • The traumatic nature of exposure to gun violence affects the health and development of young people.
  • Gun violence exposure occurs disproportionately in low-income households in disadvantaged neighborhoods.

In 2024, someone died from gun violence every 12 minutes in the United States. Gun suicides reached an all-time high, and guns remained the leading cause of death among young people (ages 1-17), with more deaths than car crashes, overdoses, or any other single cause (Kim et al., 2026).

The tragic lethality of gun violence is something that we hear or read about every day. We think less often or not at all about the more invisible but pervasive and damaging ways community violence affects those who see it happening or hear the sounds of gunfire.

The most common form of gun exposure is hearing shots in a public space, and this can create significant distress for younger children, even when the level of threat is not especially serious (Turner et al., 2019). Witnessing community violence consistently is associated with increased odds of gun carrying, substance use, and suicide risk for both males and females (Harper et al., 2023).

Exposure to gun violence is traumatic. Many researchers and clinicians, myself among them, have advocated for its inclusion in ACE (Adverse Childhood Experience) screenings. The chronic stress that arises from living in neighborhoods with high rates of gun violence triggers repeated activation of the stress response system, as other traumatic experiences do. Constant arousal of the neurobiological alarm system leads to both short- and long-term physiological and psychological consequences.

Exposure to community violence has been linked to a range of problems, including depression, post-traumatic stress, substance use, and academic difficulties in the short term, and hypertension in adulthood (Bancalari et al., 2022).

Having a gun pointed at you or being shot is different from seeing gun violence or hearing shots fired. It makes sense that the mental health symptoms that develop in response to indirect exposure to community violence are different from those that result from being directly threatened or being a victim. Witnessing violence can lead to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress (or more internalizing symptoms), whereas direct victimization can lead to externalizing symptoms of aggression, conduct disorder, and impulsivity (Bancalari et al., 2022).

There are some gender differences in symptoms. Exposure to gun violence is associated with increases in anxiety and reactive aggression among males, and symptoms of depression for females. Exposure to gun violence may have an impact on emotional regulation, perhaps increasing a tendency to perceive ambiguous social interactions as hostile in intent (Shulman et al., 2021; Leibbrand et al., 2020).

Exposure to gun violence, like other ACEs, disproportionately affects lower-income children, Black and Hispanic children, and male children (Rajan et al., 2019). The immediate community surroundings are most often the contexts that determine the likelihood of exposure. Household poverty contributes to inequities in exposure, compounding the effects of neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage (Kravitz-Wirtz, 2022).

Gun violence in the community feeds into cycles of violence by demoralizing youth, inducing gun carrying, and fostering community disorder (Bancalari, 2022). There is evidence that exposure to gun violence is correlated with a greater likelihood of gun carrying and greater peer delinquency (Shulman et al., 2021). It is easy to understand how the loss of hope in the future and the sense of danger in the neighborhood can lead young people to minimize the risks of carrying a gun. Carrying a gun increases the risk of engaging in gun violence, sometimes in cases of misidentifying a neutral encounter as a threat.

Ruben (not his real name), whom I interviewed for my book, Before Their Crimes: What We’re Misunderstanding about Childhood Trauma, Youth Crime, and the Path to Healing, had many adverse experiences early in life. Repeated exposure to gun violence was one of them, acting as a powerful catalyst in his path to delinquency and violence. He described the violence he encountered as a very young boy.

“The fear was constantly there because I would see people get hurt…the first time I witnessed cold-blooded murder, I was eight or nine years old. One of my uncles was having a party. As I’m walking up the stairs, I see an argument, and one guy pulls out a gun and shoots the other in the face. He shot another guy and ran while I was watching the two guys bleeding out…I was watching it and not feeling much about it, like it messed up my feeling fear anymore or anything much. When I was 10, I started becoming really violent, and I started trying to be in a gang.”

The degree of proximity to violence makes a difference in its impact. One study found that every additional deadly gun violence incident that occurred within 500 meters of a child’s home was associated with a 9.6% increase in youth delinquent behaviors. The further away an exposure was, the weaker were the behavioral effects (Gard et al., 2022), underscoring the fact that where you live makes all the difference to both the likelihood of exposure and the consequences to development and health that may follow.

Gun violence affects all who see or hear it. Children and young people still in the midst of development are likely to bear the brunt of its impact. Only days ago, Apple News reported that "America's gun violence decline is leaving teens behind" (Brownlee, 2026-09-17). Children and teens in violent neighborhoods express doubts about living to adulthood, which can affect not only their mental health but also their academic outcomes and their hopes for the future (Leibbrand et al., 2020).

Community violence is place-based; children who grow up in poor households in socially disadvantaged neighborhoods are most at risk. Communities need supportive strategies and place-based investments in the social, economic, and structural foundations of community life. Youth in neighborhoods with high rates of gun violence, especially those who demonstrate aggressive behavior, should be routinely screened in schools or clinics for exposure and referred to services before they turn to carrying guns themselves.

item.title: What Happens When You Become Older Than Your Older Sibling?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

What Happens When You Become Older Than Your Older Sibling?

Personal Perspective: Why "grief math" can be so disorienting.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Becoming older than our older siblings or parents were when they passed is uniquely disorienting.
  • We might be older than they got to be, but they somehow grow older alongside us.
  • It's healthy for our relationships to continue to evolve, even after our people have died.

When we're grieving, there are days we expect to be particularly hard. Our person’s birthday. The anniversary of their death. The holidays we always spent together.

And then there are the days that catch us off guard. The ones where we run into someone who hadn’t heard our person died. Or when we see someone who has an uncanny resemblance to the one we’ve lost.

But there’s another category altogether that can bring us to our knees: milestone birthdays of our own that bring us face-to-face with our loss.

I should explain at the outset that I’m a big fan of birthdays. I like being feted. I love getting presents as much as I love giving them. And I can think of nothing more celebratory than chocolate cake with lit candles waiting to be wished upon.

But this week was my birthday, and I dreaded it for a full month before. This was the birthday when I would finally reach the age my oldest sister was when she died, a turning point I simply wanted to ignore.

My sister was eight years older than me, and I grew up thinking of her as the blueprint for who I might one day become. When I was 10 and she was 18, she may as well have been a different species—not an adult like my parents, but a glamorous model of the fun and possibility that awaited me.

As we grew older, the age difference seemed to narrow. We became the best of friends, but never entirely equals. I always looked up to my sophisticated, successful big sister. And I know she looked up to me, too, even as she remained protective and always got the last word.

The idea that I would reach the age my sister was when she died was disorder in the truest sense—the opposite of order. She was supposed to always be eight years older than me. And what about next year, when I become older than her? I imagine that will feel even worse.

My identity was formed as the youngest of three sisters. The heartbreaking fact is that my other older sister died decades ago at 30, so this particular version of grief math isn’t new to me. But I don’t remember being as distraught when I became the same age as my first sister who died. Maybe that was because I still had another sister. Or maybe it’s because I was too preoccupied with trying to build a family of my own at the time. Or maybe the memory of the pain is simply one more thing that’s softened with age.

What I do know is that inside I remain the youngest of three sisters, and I’m pretty sure that will never change.

That’s the context in which I learned how to negotiate the world, how I discovered who I was and who I wanted to become. I may now be an only child on paper, but my heart tells me something different.

My sisters have both died, and I’m now nearly twice the age my first sister lived to be and with luck will soon be older than my other sister. I recognize that intellectually, but emotionally I feel something different. My sisters continue to grow alongside me. Our relationship didn’t end when their lives did. Instead, it keeps evolving as they live on not only in my memory but also as part of my DNA.

Once upon a time, we were taught that grief was something to get through—a tidy process with a beginning, middle, and end. Now we understand that staying emotionally connected to the people we’ve lost is a healthy way to move forward, hand in hand with our grief.

My sisters, frozen in time at the ages they died, grow older alongside me. I still hear their voices giving me advice and cheering me on. And I still celebrate their birthdays, because the fact that they were born is a special occasion. I picture them at the ages they were when they died, but I imagine them at the ages they’d be now, always older and a tiny bit wiser than I am.

Other times, I wallow in the sadness. I wear their sweaters or listen to the music we used to dance to together and I rage at the loss, letting the presence of their absence fill the room.

I thought my birthday would be more of the latter. I even considered ignoring it altogether, the idea of reaching my sister’s age too sad to bear. But nobody loved a party or a celebration more than she did. To ignore my excuse for cake and confetti would almost be an affront to her.

So I remembered that two things can be true, that grief and joy can live together, and that I can be the same age my sister was when she died and still keep my standing as the youngest of three.
